snip.t: Compression by a pituitary adenoma can lead to bitemporal hemianopia (due to compression of the optic chiasm), headache, hypopituitarism, and cranial nerve palsies (III, IV, VI) if the cavernous sinus is invaded.

Headache: Onset, pattern (steady vs. sudden), radiation to eyes, aggravating/relieving factors — Pituitary macroadenoma or apoplexy compresses the dura and cavernous sinus → frontal‑temporal headache; sudden “thunderclap” headache suggests apoplexy or hemorrhage.

Visual symptoms: Blurred vision, loss of peripheral vision, double vision, colour changes — Enlargement of the sellar mass compresses the optic chiasm → bitemporal hemianopia; cavernous sinus invasion can affect cranial nerves III, IV, VI → diplopia.
Cranial nerves – e.g., CN II visual field defects (optic pathway lesion), CN III‑VI palsy (brainstem or cavernous sinus pathology), CN VII facial weakness (stroke vs.
Cranial nerves: Visual field cuts, papilledema, diplopia, facial weakness — Papilledema = raised ICP; cranial nerve palsies = cavernous sinus thrombosis, HIV‑related lesions
It communicates with the cavernous sinus through the angular vein, the superior ophthalmic vein and the deep facial vein (to the pterygoid venous plexus, which connects through emissary veins).
